questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify the economic motive for empire in merchant petitions

options.text: Colonies were wanted to give crowded peasants farms in their own home countries

options.misconception: turns a request for foreign markets into a plan for a domestic cartel
options.text: Manufacturers wanted empire to end all competition between British firms

questions.explanation: Mills that outgrew home demand needed somewhere to sell cloth and somewhere cheap to buy cotton, so commercial advantage rather than charity drove the petition. options.text: Egyptian mills had outgrown British ones and were now setting the world price

options.misconception: turns a quantity series into a price story the ledgers do not give
options.text: The jump records a steep fall in world cotton prices rather than lost supply

options.misconception: puts British buyers after Egyptian independence, which came later
options.text: British buyers turned to Egypt only after Egypt had already become independent

options.text: Let each side settle its own disputes by force with no government decision at all

questions.explanation: A government that decides, and decides in public, converts two rival claims into two parties with a place in the decision, which is what makes the ruling stick where violence would only postpone it. The tempting answers award the land and create a fresh grievance, hand the colony to one group and ignore the other's shipping and credit, or refuse to decide anything at all.
questions.hint: Which side of the dispute can a judgment displease without stopping it?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: reconcile two records of resistance in one period
questions.stem: Two original summaries of the same period disagree: one lists armed risings in three regions, the other lists petitions, trials, and boycotts carried out for decades. Which synthesis best fits both?

options.text: Both forms ran at once, with revolt strongest where colonial rule was newest and weakest

options.misconception: dismisses the years of petitions the second summary records
options.text: Only the risings were real, since petitions changed no law and no mind

options.misconception: dismisses armed resistance without reading the first summary's list
options.text: Only legal agitation was real, since the risings were peasant riots led by outsiders

options.misconception: refuses a comparison both summaries share a period with
options.text: The two accounts describe different centuries and cannot be brought together at all

questions.explanation: Nothing in the two summaries makes the forms rivals: a decade of petitions in one region and a rising in a newly conquered one are different answers to how much pressure a colonial government could absorb, and each summary only records the form its own region produced. The tempting answers throw one record out or insist the two cannot be joined despite the shared period.
questions.hint: Where was colonial rule newest when these accounts were written?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: read a ledger pair as a dependency trap
questions.stem: A colonial ledger shows export crops filling the ships each year while food imports rise, and a drought then empties the interior granaries. What pattern did the export economy create?

options.text: Land and labor went to export crops, so a bad harvest abroad could starve the colony

options.misconception: denies the ledger's rising food imports alongside export growth
options.text: Food imports fell as exports rose, because both kinds of shipping were one trade

options.misconception: confuses export earnings with local nutrition under drought
options.text: The colony grew richer every year, which is why the drought went unnoticed

options.misconception: reverses the direction of grain between port and interior
options.text: Export crops fed the interior well, since local growers ate what they shipped

questions.explanation: When the best land and most labor grow what ships carry away, the colony earns foreign money and loses the food its own people eat, so a failure in world markets becomes hunger in the interior. The tempting answers contradict the rising import line in the ledger, confuse export earnings with feeding people, or send the grain the wrong way from port to village.
questions.hint: If the crop leaves the country, who eats it?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain what a freight line did that mule trains could not
questions.stem: A colonial department justified a line from an inland mining town to the coast by the cost of hauling ore by mule. Explain what that line did that the mule trains could not.

options.text: It cut the cost and time of moving heavy ore, so mines and revenue worked faster and farther

options.misconception: gives the line a relief purpose the department never claimed
options.text: It carried grain inland each season, relieving famine in the interior districts

options.misconception: credits a village aim over the stated cost of haulage
options.text: It connected scattered villages to one another, so government could rule by rail

options.misconception: confuses a freight line under construction with settler passage
options.text: It moved settlers inland, shifting the colony's population as the line opened

questions.explanation: Mule haulage cost scales with weight and distance, so a railway cut the charge per ton until ore worth mining at one profit could be shipped at all, which enlarged both the mines and the revenue they paid. The tempting answers give the line purposes the department's own justification denies: relief, village links, and passenger traffic are effects it never claimed.
questions.hint: Why does a line change the price of moving heavy stone?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Notification in the partition of Africa
questions.learningObjective: identify the rule that made claiming territory cheap
questions.stem: An original summary of a European diplomatic conference records that coastal territory could be claimed once the other powers had been notified, that claims on the same river valley were shared, and that an occupying power must inform rivals before trading. Which rule made claiming cheap?

options.text: Notification instead of consent, so land could be taken by informing rivals afterwards

options.misconception: inverts notification into a veto the conference never granted
options.text: Consent by every power before occupation, so nothing could be claimed without agreement

options.misconception: claims a prohibition the conference plainly did not issue
options.text: A ban on any African territory, leaving the continent to its own rulers alone

options.misconception: invents a permanent court no summary of the meeting mentions
options.text: A shared supreme court, so every disputed claim got one settled ruling

questions.explanation: Once taking possession is enough as long as the others are told afterwards, a power with ships and a small landing party can put a claim on the map for the cost of the voyage, which is why the scramble went so far in so few years. The tempting answers turn notice into consent, or read into the conference a prohibition and a court that no summary of it records.
questions.hint: Did the rule require permission, or only a letter?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: weigh two verdicts on imperial rivalry together
questions.stem: Two original summaries weigh the same rivalry: one credits it with fast fleets, steady finances, and skilled staffs, the other with rising budgets, colonial quarrels, and hard bargaining at every crisis. Which synthesis joins them?

options.text: Competition armed states well, but the same rivalry made a cheap settlement impossible

options.misconception: ignores the bargaining and budgets the second summary records
options.text: Competition produced only benefits, since rivalries never led to any confrontation

options.misconception: reduces European spending to a colonial matter the first summary denies
options.text: Competition was only a colonial matter, with no effect on budgets in Europe

options.misconception: calls contradiction what is really two sides of one record
options.text: The records contradict each other, so no historian can rank their claims

questions.explanation: Rivalry built the means of war, fast ships and reliable credit, and simultaneously raised the price of any disagreement, since every power had too much at stake to concede quietly. The tempting answers keep only the benefits, push the whole effect into the colonies, or read two complementary verdicts as a contradiction that cancels them out.
questions.hint: Can the same competition build armies and prevent agreement?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: trace how empire built the forces that undid it
questions.stem: Pupils in colonial schools, officers trained abroad, and a ruined treasury in Europe all pointed one way by 1945. Explain how the same system that built these empires made them hard to hold.

answer.exemplar: Each empire spent decades training educated men it then excluded from power, teaching them that their country's claims were unjust while Europe claimed the same rights, and by 1945 the war that finished Europe had left the imperial powers too few men and too much debt to hold far-flung territories. The trained locals turned the language of civilization and national rights against the rule that had used both.

questions.explanation: A strong answer joins three threads: education created a class the colony then denied a share in power, war debts and demobilization removed the resources to garrison the empire, and the vocabulary of national self-determination supplied an argument the colonizer had itself used in Europe.
questions.hint: Who was trained in the colonizer's own schools, and for what?
